endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Source code and model escrow: For high-risk or critical patient safety solutions, require escrow of model weights, inference code, documentation, and/or runbooks, with release triggers tied to vendor failure events.

endorsements.title: Adoption of AI in Healthcare Delivery Systems: Early Applications and Impacts
endorsements.quote: As clinicians increasingly rely on AI-generated notes rather than writing their own, a reevaluation of training protocols to ensure clinicians have the skills to effectively review AI-generated documentation is needed.

endorsements.title: California AB 3030 (2024), generative AI in patient communications
endorsements.quote: (b) If a communication is generated by generative artificial intelligence and read and reviewed by a human licensed or certified health care provider, the requirements of subdivision (a) do not apply.

endorsements.title: Guardrails for GenAI drafted replies in patient portal messaging
endorsements.issuer: Sakr J. npj Digital Medicine 2026;9 (PMID 41942581, doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02621-6)
endorsements.quote: - Tier 2 (moderate risk): clinician must edit at least one clinically meaningful element (e.g., assessment/plan or red-flag instructions) before send.

endorsements.title: Generative AI for pre-consultation mental health triage in disorders of gut-brain interaction
endorsements.quote: Once intake is completed, the system can generate a draft summary for review, but no patient-facing conclusions should be issued without clinician approval.

endorsements.title: Reclaiming the Human Connection in Clinical Care With AI
endorsements.quote: AI-generated draft responses and summaries must be reviewed and edited by the clinician before use; and provider training should cover not only how to use these tools but how to critically evaluate their outputs.

evidence.title: A Comparative Study of Responses to Retina Questions from Either Experts, Expert-Edited Large Language Models, or Expert-Edited Large Language Models Alone
evidence.outcome: Safety metrics of expert-edited LLM drafts versus expert-written and unedited LLM responses
evidence.effect: Expert-edited drafts (Expert + AI) had higher quality and empathy than Expert alone, but were worse than Expert on most safety metrics; e.g. incorrect content low risk 0.801 vs 0.832, with 2% high-risk vs 0%.
evidence.quote: In terms of safety metrics, utilizing the established methodology from Singhal et al 17 allows for comparisons, where Expert + AI performed worse than Expert in all metrics except missing content.

evidence.title: Opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in patient portal messaging in primary care
evidence.outcome: Whether physician review of AI-drafted patient messages caught and corrected embedded errors
evidence.effect: Each erroneous draft was missed by 13-15 of 20 PCPs; 35-45% submitted unedited; only one participant addressed all four errors; mean 2.67 of 4 missed.
evidence.quote: Each erroneous AI draft was “missed” by at least 13 participants (65%) and was submitted entirely unedited by at least seven participants (35%).

evidence.title: Assessing the Accuracy and Reliability of ChatGPT-4 to Answer Clinical EHR Messages in Sports Medicine
evidence.outcome: Physician-rated acceptability and harm potential of LLM drafts when reviewed before sending
evidence.effect: Physicians rated LLM-assisted responses acceptable without modifications in 58/80 (72.50%); unedited drafts had low chance of harm in 75/80 (93.75%), so 22/80 needed edits before being safe to send.
evidence.quote: In stage 2, the physicians rated the LLM-assisted responses as acceptable without modifications in 58 out of 80 cases (72.50%).
evidence.sample_unit: synthetic EHR patient message scenarios with LLM drafts

evidence.title: Radiologist Detection of Deficiencies in LLM-Generated Patient Communications About Radiology Reports: A Multi-Reader Study
evidence.venue: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
evidence.outcome: Whether clinician review catches errors in LLM patient-facing answers, single vs multi-reader
evidence.effect: Single reader missed an average of 12.4% of deficiencies; dual-reader review reduced average miss rate to 0.6%; triple-reader detected all.
evidence.quote: A single reader missed an average of 12.4% of deficiencies, whereas dual-reader review reduced the average miss rate to 0.6%; triple-reader review detected all deficiencies.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM-generated answers to simulated patient questions

evidence.title: Clinician-supervised large language AI model after-discharge instruction generation for common emergency department presentations
evidence.effect: Physician edits improved accuracy but reduced objective readability scores.
evidence.quote: Physician edits improved accuracy but paradoxically reduced objective readability scores.

evidence.title: Physician-revised AI-generated drafts are associated with higher ratings of written explanations in end-of-life care in the intensive care unit: a scenario-based single-center cross-sectional study
evidence.outcome: Rated medical validity and empathy of physician-revised LLM drafts versus AI-only and physician-only responses
evidence.effect: Physician-AI collaborative responses rated higher than AI-only and physician-only for medical validity (median 4.0 vs 3.5 and 3.7) and empathy (HCP 4.3 vs 3.2 and 3.2); all P<0.001 in primary analyses (non-HCP empathy P=0.019).
evidence.quote: In the primary analyses, physician–AI collaborative responses received higher ratings than both physician-only and AI-only responses across all three primary outcomes.

evidence.title: Prompt engineering on leveraging large language models in generating response to InBasket messages
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Hallucinated clinical information in AI-drafted patient message replies
evidence.effect: 7 (6%) of 116 training-set drafts contained hallucinated information; none in the validation set; 16% of validation drafts rejected by physicians.
evidence.quote: Interesting, 7 (6%) of the 116 original messages from the test set were found to contain hallucinated information in the LLM responses.

evidence.title: Comparing ChatGPT and a Single Anesthesiologist's Responses to Common Patient Questions: An Exploratory Cross-Sectional Survey of a Panel of Anesthesiologists
evidence.outcome: Rate of possible harm in ChatGPT-drafted answers versus anesthesiologist answers, rated by blinded anesthesiologists
evidence.effect: Possibility of harm 4.7% for ChatGPT vs 1.7% for the anesthesiologist (p = .04); agreement with scientific consensus 96.6% vs 99.3% (p = .02).
evidence.quote: ChatGPT underperformed the anesthesiologist regarding rate of responses in agreement with scientific consensus (96.6% vs. 99.3%, p = .02) and possibility of harm (4.7% vs. 1.7%, p = .04), but performed similarly in other measures (percentage of responses with inappropriate/incorrect information (5.7% vs. 2.7%, p = .07) and missing information (10.0% vs. 7.0%, p = .19)).

evidence.title: Prompt matters: evaluation of large language model chatbot responses related to Peyronie's disease
evidence.quote: LLMs were accurate and complete, with average scores of 5.5 of 6.0 (SD, 0.8) and 2.8 of 3.0 (SD, 0.4), respectively ( Table 2 ).
evidence.sample_unit: chatbot responses (9 NIH FAQs prompted/unprompted and 11 simulated presurgical messages across 4 LLMs; 254 citations)

evidence.title: Application of AI Chatbot in Responding to Asynchronous Text-Based Messages From Patients With Cancer: Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: Potentially adverse-outcome rate of chatbot vs physician responses in medical decision-making
evidence.effect: 3.12% (59/1893) of chatbot responses potentially leading to adverse outcomes vs 2.01% (38/1893) for physicians; lower accuracy (96.88% vs 97.99%, P<.001) in decision-making scenario.
evidence.quote: Errors in chatbot responses were primarily due to misinterpretations of medical terminology or the lack of updated guidelines, with 3.12% (59/1893) of its responses potentially leading to adverse outcomes, compared with 2.01% (38/1893) for physicians.
evidence.sample_unit: deidentified asynchronous text-based medical consultation records

evidence.title: Can ChatGPT provide responses to patients for orthopaedic-related questions? A comparison between ChatGPT and medical support staff
evidence.outcome: High-risk errors in ChatGPT-generated replies to patient questions
evidence.effect: Three ChatGPT responses showed high-risk errors among 50 compared, with no difference from support staff in risk of incorrect treatment (p = 0.377).
evidence.quote: Three ChatGPT responses showed high-risk errors.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence Can Answer Postoperative Questions About Distal Radius Fractures-But Can Patients Understand the Answers?
evidence.venue: Journal of hand surgery global online
evidence.outcome: Safety and appropriateness of AI responses to postoperative questions as judged by reviewers
evidence.effect: Two reviewers deemed all responses from the three platforms safe and appropriate; DISCERN 54 (ChatGPT), 69 (Copilot), 63 (Gemini).
evidence.quote: The two reviewers deemed all responses as safe and appropriate.

evidence.title: Accuracy and Readability of Chat Generative Pre-Trained Transformer-4 Omni in Answering Ophthalmology Patient Questions
evidence.outcome: Incomplete or unacceptable AI patient replies
evidence.effect: Standard ChatGPT-4o replies: 220/285 (77.2%) accurate and complete, 49 (17.2%) incomplete, 16 (5.6%) unacceptable.
evidence.quote: Overall, 220 (77%) responses were graded as accurate and complete, 49 (17%) as incomplete, and 16 (6%) as unacceptable.

evidence.title: A Novel Workflow for Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Patient Messaging Services
evidence.effect: Consequential additions occurred in 3.36% and omissions in 1.12% of AI-enhanced messages.
evidence.quote: Safety analysis identified consequential additions in 3.36% and omissions in 1.12% of AI-enhanced messages.

evidence.title: Large Language Model-Generated Patient Instructions for Prescriptions in Primary Health Care: Preclinical Algorithm Validation
evidence.effect: Incorrect-use instructions: ChatGPT n=15 (22.7%), Llama n=19 (22.8%), Llama-RAG n=19 (22.8%); P=.71.
evidence.quote: Instructions leading to incorrect use of the medication had similar frequency among the models(ChatGPT-4.0: n=15, 22.7%; Llama3.1-8B: n=19, 22.8%; Llama3.1-8B-RAG: n=19, 22.8%; chi-square test P=.71).
evidence.sample_unit: evaluations of LLM-generated instructions by 62 primary health care prescribers

evidence.title: Correctness, Harmfulness, and Diversity of Large Language Models for Colonoscopy Preparation Assistance: Comparative Evaluation Study
evidence.effect: Human harmfulness rates before filtering: Mistral 33/251 (13.1%), Llama 30/237 (12.7%), GPT-4.1 9/250 (3.6%), o3 10/231 (4.3%).
evidence.quote: All models produced harmful errors, primarily due to omissions or misinterpretations of prep instructions.
evidence.sample_unit: synthetic dialogues per model (50 per model human-rated)

commentary.bottom_line: Six simulated studies tested clinician review of AI-drafted patient messages, and their results conflict: review raised rated validity and empathy in some, while physicians missed most embedded errors in another. No study measured patient harm in live use, so single-clinician review may not reliably stop unsafe messages.

perspectives.view: All six tests are level 4 vignette or replay studies in offline settings. Sample sizes ranged from 8 presentations to 1200 answers. Two studies support the practice, one points against it, and three are mixed. Certainty starts low and drops to very low because the settings are indirect, the findings are inconsistent, and most samples are small.

Each erroneous draft was missed by 13 to 15 of 20 physicians, and only one physician caught all four errors. Expert-edited drafts carried 2% high-risk incorrect content versus 0% for expert-written replies. A single reader missed 12.4% of deficiencies, and a second reader reduced misses to 0.6%. Single review may let errors reach patients.

Between 35% and 45% of physicians submitted erroneous drafts unedited, which suggests that reviewers may accept what the draft says. In a separate test, physicians judged 72.50% of drafts acceptable without changes, and 22 of 80 needed edits before they were safe to send. No study measured review fidelity in real workflows.

Physician edits to discharge instructions improved accuracy but lowered objective readability scores. This trade-off may matter for patients with low literacy. A Japanese study found that physician-revised drafts scored higher on validity and empathy. That study covers non-English communication, but it does not include U.S. patients with limited English proficiency.

California AB 3030 states that the requirements of its subdivision (a) do not apply when a licensed or certified provider reads and reviews an AI-generated communication. The supplied excerpt does not say how thorough that review must be. The CHAI excerpt concerns model escrow rather than clinician review, so it offers no direct support for this recommendation.

Dual-reader review reduced the average miss rate from 12.4% to 0.6%, and triple review detected every deficiency. Each added reader would add clinician time per message. None of the six studies reported review time or staffing cost, so the burden at scale cannot be estimated from this evidence.

In one test, expert-edited drafts were rated higher on quality and empathy than expert-written replies but performed worse on most safety metrics. This suggests that warmer wording and accurate content may not travel together. A message that reads well after clinician approval may still contain errors that a patient cannot detect.

commentary.research_gap: No study tested clinician review in a live portal deployment with patient harm, near misses, or clinician time as outcomes. No study compared single review with dual review, or with tiered edit requirements, inside real workflows. Training interventions for reviewers also remain untested.
commentary.underserved_note: One test included non-English communication (Japan), and none included Medicaid, safety-net, U.S. limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The finding that physician edits reduced readability suggests that review could make messages harder for low-literacy patients to use, and that possibility has not been studied in those groups.
